claim: Microbial colonies are structures in which growth and internal organization reflect complex morphogenetic processes.
source: Microbial colonies are fascinating structures in which growth and internal organization reflect complex morphogenetic processes.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's context.

claim: Stable glucose gradients emerge in yeast monolayer colonies.
source: We observed the emergence of stable glucose gradients using fluorescently labeled hexose transporters and quantified the spatial correlations with intra-colony growth rates and expression of other genes regulated by glucose availability.
evidence: The abstract states this as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Glucose gradients can be observed using fluorescently labeled hexose transporters.
source: We observed the emergence of stable glucose gradients using fluorescently labeled hexose transporters and quantified the spatial correlations with intra-colony growth rates and expression of other genes regulated by glucose availability.
evidence: The abstract describes the methodology used to observe glucose gradients.

claim: Glucose gradient landscapes depend on external glucose concentration.
source: These landscapes depended on the external glucose concentration as well as secondary gradients, for example amino acid availability.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding about the factors affecting landscape formation.

claim: Glucose gradient landscapes depend on amino acid availability.
source: These landscapes depended on the external glucose concentration as well as secondary gradients, for example amino acid availability.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding about the factors affecting landscape formation.

claim: Regulatory genetic networks governing cellular physiological adaptation are key to internal structuration of cellular assemblies.
source: This work demonstrates the regulatory genetic networks governing cellular physiological adaptation are the key to internal structuration of cellular assemblies.
evidence: The abstract presents this as a conclusion from the work.

claim: Cells at the outskirts of a multicellular assembly experience a different microenvironment than cells deeply buried within.
source: Thus, cells at the outskirts of a multicellular assembly do not experience the same microenvironment as the cells deeply buried within.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction based on the fact that cells create spatial gradients.

claim: Cellular physiology is dependent on the cell's position within a colony.
source: Reciprocally, cellular physiology is dependent on the cell's position within a colony.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: Variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in bacterial and yeast colonies.
source: Such variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in a variety of multicellular systems – from bacterial and yeast colonies (Vulin et al., 2014; Cáp et al., 2012) to biofilms (Nadell et al., 2016) and tumors (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013; Delarue et al., 2014) – and are reflected by altered gene expression levels and cellular phenotypes as growth rates, nutrient uptake rates and metabolic activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in biofilms.
source: Such variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in a variety of multicellular systems – from bacterial and yeast colonies (Vulin et al., 2014; Cáp et al., 2012) to biofilms (Nadell et al., 2016) and tumors (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013; Delarue et al., 2014) – and are reflected by altered gene expression levels and cellular phenotypes as growth rates, nutrient uptake rates and metabolic activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in tumors.
source: Such variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in a variety of multicellular systems – from bacterial and yeast colonies (Vulin et al., 2014; Cáp et al., 2012) to biofilms (Nadell et al., 2016) and tumors (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013; Delarue et al., 2014) – and are reflected by altered gene expression levels and cellular phenotypes as growth rates, nutrient uptake rates and metabolic activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Variations in cellular physiology are reflected by altered gene expression levels and cellular phenotypes.
source: Such variations in cellular physiology are consistently observed in a variety of multicellular systems – from bacterial and yeast colonies (Vulin et al., 2014; Cáp et al., 2012) to biofilms (Nadell et al., 2016) and tumors (Carmona-Fontaine et al., 2013; Delarue et al., 2014) – and are reflected by altered gene expression levels and cellular phenotypes as growth rates, nutrient uptake rates and metabolic activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Variations in cellular physiology emerge because of long-range metabolic interactions between cells.
source: Such variations presumably emerge because of long-range metabolic interactions between cells, in that the cellular microenvironment at one position depends on the nutrient uptake rate at another position.
evidence: This is presented as a presumption or hypothesis in the introduction.

claim: Multicellular communities exhibit higher cell proliferation as an adaptive benefit.
source: Notably, multicellular communities (Shapiro, 1998; Shou et al., 2007; Xavier and Foster, 2007) exhibit various adaptive benefits, including higher cell proliferation, improved access to resources and niches (Koschwanez et al., 2011), collective defence (e.g., against antagonists, drugs, antibiotics) (Nadell et al., 2016) resulting in optimization of population survival when confronted with averse physical, chemical, nutritional or biological challenges (Palková and Váchová, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Multicellular communities exhibit improved access to resources and niches as an adaptive benefit.
source: Notably, multicellular communities (Shapiro, 1998; Shou et al., 2007; Xavier and Foster, 2007) exhibit various adaptive benefits, including higher cell proliferation, improved access to resources and niches (Koschwanez et al., 2011), collective defence (e.g., against antagonists, drugs, antibiotics) (Nadell et al., 2016) resulting in optimization of population survival when confronted with averse physical, chemical, nutritional or biological challenges (Palková and Váchová, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Multicellular communities exhibit collective defence as an adaptive benefit.
source: Notably, multicellular communities (Shapiro, 1998; Shou et al., 2007; Xavier and Foster, 2007) exhibit various adaptive benefits, including higher cell proliferation, improved access to resources and niches (Koschwanez et al., 2011), collective defence (e.g., against antagonists, drugs, antibiotics) (Nadell et al., 2016) resulting in optimization of population survival when confronted with averse physical, chemical, nutritional or biological challenges (Palková and Váchová, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The majority of scientific research to date has focused on single cells in homogeneous environments or populations of cells grown in batch or continuous liquid cultures.
source: Yet, despite the obvious contrast between homogeneous environments and the pronounced environmental heterogeneity of microbial cellular assemblies, the majority of scientific research to date has either focused on single cells in homogeneous environments or populations of cells grown in batch or continuous liquid cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation about the state of the field.

claim: Two-photon microscopy of sliced agarose-encapsulated yeast colonies was required to show that yeast cells may adopt different physiologies depending on their position within a colony.
source: For example, two-photon microscopy of sliced agarose-encapsulated yeast colonies was required to show that yeast cells may adopt different physiologies – and possibly different cell types – depending on their position within a colony (Cáp et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Yeast cells may adopt different physiologies depending on their position within a colony.
source: For example, two-photon microscopy of sliced agarose-encapsulated yeast colonies was required to show that yeast cells may adopt different physiologies – and possibly different cell types – depending on their position within a colony (Cáp et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: NanoDESI MS was used to study growing bacterial colonies on agar plates and showed a wide diversity and complexity of compounds that characterize microbial chemical ecology.
source: In another example, nanospray desorption electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (nanoDESI MS) was used to study growing bacterial colonies on agar plates and showed a wide diversity and complexity of compounds that characterize microbial chemical ecology (Watrous et al., 2012; Traxler and Kolter, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The microfluidic device has dead-end chambers that are 800 µm long, 50 µm wide, and 4.5 µm high.
source: We used soft lithography techniques to fabricate a multi-layered microfluidic device composed of a large channel (to flow nutrients) and an array of perpendicular, extended (800 µm-long), narrow (50 µm-wide), flat (4.5 µm-high) dead-end chambers in which yeast cells can grow as monolayers while the media is supplied by a pressure pump-based system with flow control (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the physical specifications of the device used in the study.

claim: The length of the dead-end chambers was optimized to induce significant variations in the nutrient concentrations within the chambers due to cellular nutrient uptake.
source: The length of the dead-end chambers was optimized to induce significant variations in the nutrient concentrations within the chambers due to cellular nutrient uptake.
evidence: This describes a design consideration for the device.

claim: The chamber width was large enough to avoid jamming during cell growth due to geometric constraints.
source: The chamber width was large enough to avoid jamming during cell growth due to geometric constraints and small enough to avoid generation of complex, cell-recirculating flows induced by cell growth (Boyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes a design consideration for the device.

claim: The chamber width was small enough to avoid generation of complex, cell-recirculating flows induced by cell growth.
source: The chamber width was large enough to avoid jamming during cell growth due to geometric constraints and small enough to avoid generation of complex, cell-recirculating flows induced by cell growth (Boyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes a design consideration for the device, supported by a citation.

claim: The chamber height was comparable to but slightly larger than the average size of a yeast cell.
source: The chamber height was comparable to – but slightly larger than – the average size of a yeast cell, so the cells were vertically constrained to facilitate single-cell imaging and time-lapse fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a design consideration for the device.

claim: Cells formed growing monolayers that extended from the closed end of the chamber and collectively progressed towards the nutrient source.
source: The cells formed growing monolayers that extended from the closed end of the chamber and collectively progressed towards the nutrient source (i.e. the open end of the chamber) as the cells pushed each other while growing (Figure 2a,b; Video 1).
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiments, supported by figures and video.

claim: Cells eventually filled each chamber, forming an extended two-dimensional colony composed of about 2500 cells.
source: Cells eventually filled each chamber, forming an extended two-dimensional colony composed of about 2500 cells (Figure 2b, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), typically ~10 cells wide and ~200 cells long.
evidence: This describes an observation from the experiments, supported by figures.

claim: Under standard glucose-rich conditions (2% w/vol; 111 mM) and excess amino acids (5× CSM), the front velocity increased during the first 2-4 h and eventually reached a steady-state close to 100 µm.h−1.
source: Under standard glucose-rich conditions (2% w/vol; 111 mM) and excess amino acids (5× CSM, see Materials and methods), the front velocity, VF, increased during the first 2-4 h and eventually reached a steady-state close to 100 µm.h−1 (Figure 2c,d, Video 1).
evidence: This describes a specific experimental observation, supported by figures and video.

claim: Front velocity depends on the quantities of glucose and other nutrients that penetrate inside the yeast monolayer.
source: Front velocity is the sum of the contribution of every cell to colony expansion. Therefore, VF depends on the quantities of glucose and other nutrients that penetrate inside the yeast monolayer, which impact both the number of cells that grow and their growth rates.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between front velocity and nutrient availability.

claim: The glucose penetration distance is around 400 µm at 2% w/vol glucose.
source: Our direct observation (Figure 2e) showed that for a layer of growing cells, H is around 400 µm at 2% w/vol glucose.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiments, supported by a figure.

claim: Increasing the glucose concentration (from 0.01% to 8% w/vol) led to higher terminal front velocities.
source: Increasing the glucose concentration (from 0.01% to 8% w/vol) led to higher terminal front velocities (Figure 2d), in agreement with the fact that at higher concentrations, glucose will penetrate further by diffusion in the colony (Figure 2a).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation, supported by figures.

claim: The front velocity does not increase linearly with glucose concentration, and plateaus at very high glucose concentrations (>4% w/vol).
source: Yet, the front velocity does not increase linearly with glucose concentration, and plateaus at very high glucose concentrations (>4% w/vol).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: Using standard amino acid concentrations in the media resulted in significantly lower terminal front velocities, even at high glucose concentrations.
source: Indeed, using standard amino acid concentrations in the media resulted in significantly lower terminal front velocities, even at high glucose concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation, supported by a figure.

claim: Amino acid availability can limit cellular growth, which is especially visible in the presence of high glucose concentrations.
source: This suggests that amino acid availability can limit cellular growth, which is especially visible in the presence of high glucose concentrations, where glucose is no longer limiting but amino acids are.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: At standard glucose conditions (2% w/vol) and a high amino acid concentration (5 × CSM), significant cell motion was not observed after y ~ 400 µm.
source: At standard glucose conditions (2% w/vol) and a high amino acid concentration (5 × CSM), significant cell motion was not observed after y ~ 400 µm, indicating that very limited glucose is available to the cells that are beyond this region.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: Increasing the glucose concentration in the nutrient channel (from 0.01% to 8% w/vol) led to higher local velocities deeper in the colony.
source: As expected, increasing the glucose concentration in the nutrient channel (from 0.01% to 8% w/vol) led to higher local velocities deeper in the colony (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation, supported by figures.

claim: HXT1 and HXT7 displayed inversely correlated landscapes of gene expression.
source: In particular, HXT1 and HXT7 displayed inversely correlated landscapes of gene expression (e.g., Figure 3a and g for 2% w/vol glucose).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation, supported by figures.

claim: HXT1 is a low-affinity glucose transporter mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions.
source: HXT1 is a low-affinity glucose transporter mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions, while HXT7 is a high-affinity glucose transporter expressed under low-glucose conditions only (Figure 3b and f) (Reifenberger et al., 1997; Diderich et al., 1999; Maier et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and figures from the current study.

claim: HXT7 is a high-affinity glucose transporter expressed under low-glucose conditions only.
source: HXT1 is a low-affinity glucose transporter mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions, while HXT7 is a high-affinity glucose transporter expressed under low-glucose conditions only (Figure 3b and f) (Reifenberger et al., 1997; Diderich et al., 1999; Maier et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies and figures from the current study.

claim: HXT1 was expressed at the highest levels in the cells close to the chamber opening.
source: Concomitantly, HXT1 was expressed at the highest levels in the cells close to the chamber opening (i.e., in the highest glucose concentration), while HXT7 expression peaked further away in the chamber, indicating a transition to a low-glucose region.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: HXT7 expression peaked further away in the chamber, indicating a transition to a low-glucose region.
source: Concomitantly, HXT1 was expressed at the highest levels in the cells close to the chamber opening (i.e., in the highest glucose concentration), while HXT7 expression peaked further away in the chamber, indicating a transition to a low-glucose region.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference.

claim: In cells expressing the highest levels of HXT7, the fluorescence was localized to the cell membrane, indicating HTX7 played an active role in glucose transport in these cells.
source: As expected, in the cells expressing the highest levels of this gene, the fluorescence was localized to the cell membrane, indicating HTX7 played an active role in glucose transport in these cells.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference.

claim: Deeper in the colony, lower levels of HTX7 fluorescence were observed, though this fluorescence was localized in vacuoles, indicating the transporter had been targeted for degradation by the cells.
source: In contrast, deeper in the colony, we observed lower levels of HTX7 fluorescence due to the long lifetime of GFP-fused proteins and absence of dilution through cell division, though this fluorescence was localized in vacuoles, indicating the transporter had been targeted for degradation by the cells (Hovsepian et al., 2017) (Figure 3a).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by a citation and figure.

claim: The peak of HXT7 fluorescence matches the peak fluorescence observed in batch culture at a glucose concentration of 0.016% w/vol.
source: Assuming the observed peak of HXT7 fluorescence matches the peak fluorescence observed in batch culture at a glucose concentration of 0.016% w/vol. (Figure 3b,c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), we could locate the position in the yeast monolayer at which the glucose concentration reached 0.016% w/vol.
evidence: This is an assumption used to infer glucose concentrations, supported by figures.

claim: The position at which the glucose concentration reached 0.016% w/vol was around Hf ~ 500 µm from the front.
source: This position was around Hf ~ 500 µm from the front, in good agreement with the transition in cell motion (Figure 2, Hm ~400 µm).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data, supported by figures.

claim: At 1% w/vol glucose, HXT1 was only expressed at low levels at the growing front of the colony (y < 60 µm).
source: In particular, at 1% w/vol glucose, HXT1 was only expressed at low levels at the growing front of the colony (y < 60 µm).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: At the highest glucose concentration (8% w/vol), HXT1 was expressed at high levels throughout the whole colony, demonstrating glucose was available throughout the chamber.
source: In contrast, at the highest glucose concentration (8% w/vol; Figure 3e, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), HXT1 was expressed at high levels throughout the whole colony, demonstrating glucose was available throughout the chamber.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by figures.

claim: HXT1 is mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions (>1% w/vol glucose) in batch culture.
source: As HXT1 is mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions (>1% w/vol glucose) in batch culture (Diderich et al., 1999), this observation indicated the glucose penetration distance (within the chamber) increased with the external glucose concentration.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The glucose penetration distance increased with the external glucose concentration.
source: As HXT1 is mainly expressed under high-glucose conditions (>1% w/vol glucose) in batch culture (Diderich et al., 1999), this observation indicated the glucose penetration distance (within the chamber) increased with the external glucose concentration.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental observations.

claim: HXT7 exhibited a peak-like expression pattern, and was repressed under both high-glucose conditions and when no glucose was present.
source: In contrast, HXT7 exhibited a peak-like expression pattern, and was repressed under both high-glucose conditions and when no glucose was present.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: At low-glucose concentrations (0.1% w/vol), a peak in HXT7 expression was observed at the very beginning of the colony (y ~ 20 µm).
source: At low-glucose concentrations (0.1% w/vol), a peak in HXT7 expression was observed at the very beginning of the colony (y ~ 20 µm), indicating glucose was quickly absorbed by the cells closest to the chamber opening, thus these were the only cells with access to sufficient carbon resources to grow and divide.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference.

claim: The peak of HXT7 expression moved deeper into the colony as the glucose concentration increased.
source: The peak of HXT7 expression moved deeper into the colony as the glucose concentration increased and disappeared completely at 8% w/vol glucose, again indicating sufficient glucose could diffuse to the end of the chamber under high-glucose conditions (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by figures.

claim: The peak of HXT7 expression disappeared completely at 8% w/vol glucose, indicating sufficient glucose could diffuse to the end of the chamber under high-glucose conditions.
source: The peak of HXT7 expression moved deeper into the colony as the glucose concentration increased and disappeared completely at 8% w/vol glucose, again indicating sufficient glucose could diffuse to the end of the chamber under high-glucose conditions (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by figures.

claim: The local level of HXT7 expression is only set by the local glucose concentration.
source: Assuming that the local level of HXT7 expression is only set by the local glucose concentration, we can use batch culture measurements of HXT7 expression (based on flow cytometry) to determine the glucose concentration at a given chamber position (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is an assumption used for the analysis.

claim: Using HXT7 expression data allows reconstruction of the glucose gradient for different initial glucose concentrations.
source: Using the data for HXT7 in Figure 3, we were able to reconstruct the glucose gradient for different initial glucose concentrations (Figure 4e).
evidence: This describes a method and result from the study, supported by figures.

claim: When applied to HXT1, the same inference led to very similar results as HXT7.
source: When applied to HXT1, the same inference led to very similar results (Figure 4f).
evidence: This describes a result from the study, supported by a figure.

claim: Glucose concentrations decay very quickly moving away from the chamber opening and then exhibit a relatively long tail moving deeper into the colony.
source: In both cases, glucose concentrations decay very quickly moving away from the chamber opening and then exhibit a relatively long tail moving deeper into the colony.
evidence: This describes a pattern observed in the reconstructed glucose gradients.

claim: MIG1 is a key transcription factor involved in glucose repression that localizes to the nucleus in the presence of glucose.
source: MIG1 is a key transcription factor involved in glucose repression that localizes to the nucleus in the presence of glucose, to repress genes that participate in parallel carbon metabolic pathways (e.g., galactose) (Conrad et al., 2014; Broach, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The distance after which MIG1 fluorescence was not present in the nucleus of the cells was around 400 µm at C0 = 2% w/vol glucose.
source: Observing the cells at high magnification, we quantified the distance after which MIG1 fluorescence was not present in the nucleus of the cells (Figure 5b). This distance, around 400 µm at C0 = 2% w/vol glucose, was in excellent agreement with the data obtained by HXT7 profiling.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation, supported by a figure.

claim: The spatial transition from nuclear MIG1 to cytoplasmic MIG1 localisation was very sharp and occurred over just a few cells.
source: Interestingly, the spatial transition from nuclear MIG1 to cytoplasmic MIG1 localisation was very sharp and occurred over just a few cells.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: HXT5 is expressed under very low and no glucose conditions and appears to be a good marker of growth arrest.
source: In agreement with the batch culture observations, we found HXT5 was only expressed in regions with very low or no glucose concentrations where the cells did not seem to divide over several hours (Figure 5a). Therefore, HXT5 appears to be an excellent marker of growth arrest in this context (Verwaal et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by a figure and citation.

claim: The expression landscapes of HXK1 and HXK2 were consistent with the batch measurements and validated the existence of a glucose gradient.
source: The expression landscapes of two hexokinases involved in glucose metabolism, HXK1 and HXK2 (Figure 5c) that are expressed when cells are grown on non-glucose carbon sources, were also consistent with the batch measurements (Figure 5d, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) and further validated the existence of a glucose gradient.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by figures.

claim: Maximal HXK1 and HXK2 expression were observed at a glucose concentration of about 0.016% w/vol in batch measurements.
source: The batch measurements indicated maximal HXK1 and HXK2 expression were observed at a glucose concentration of about 0.016% w/vol.
evidence: This describes a result from batch culture measurements.

claim: Neither HXK1 nor HXK2 was expressed at very high glucose concentrations.
source: As expected, neither enzyme was expressed at very high glucose concentrations.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: The HXK1 and HXK2 expression maxima were around 300 µm at C0 = 1% and 500 µm at 2% w/vol.
source: The HXK1 and HXK2 expression maxima were similar at the two other glucose concentrations studied, around 300 µm at C0 = 1% and 500 µm at 2% w/vol.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation.

claim: PDC1 and SDH2 expression landscapes were inversely correlated, indicating a transition from fermentative metabolic activity at the nutrient front of the colony to respiratory metabolic activity towards the dead end of the chamber.
source: Finally, we examined the expression of PDC1 and SDH2, which are overexpressed in fermenting and respiring cells, respectively (Otterstedt et al., 2004; Bonander et al., 2008; Ohlmeier et al., 2004). Their expression landscapes were inversely correlated (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating a transition from fermentative metabolic activity at the nutrient front of the colony to respiratory metabolic activity towards the dead end of the chamber where glucose is scarce.
evidence: This describes an experimental observation and inference, supported by figures and citations.

claim: PDC1 is overexpressed in fermenting cells.
source: Finally, we examined the expression of PDC1 and SDH2, which are overexpressed in fermenting and respiring cells, respectively (Otterstedt et al., 2004; Bonander et al., 2008; Ohlmeier et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: SDH2 is overexpressed in respiring cells.
source: Finally, we examined the expression of PDC1 and SDH2, which are overexpressed in fermenting and respiring cells, respectively (Otterstedt et al., 2004; Bonander et al., 2008; Ohlmeier et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: All gene expression landscapes showed a high level of spatial correlation.
source: We decided to compare the landscapes of gene expression for the entire set of reporter genes by aligning the different landscapes across varied nutrient conditions (Figure 7a). Strikingly, all landscapes showed a high level of spatial correlation.
evidence: This describes an observation from comparing multiple gene expression landscapes, supported by a figure.

claim: Two major landscape types emerged: peaking (e.g., HXT7) and switching (e.g., HXT1 or MIG1).
source: Two major landscapes emerged: peaking (e.g., HXT7) and switching (e.g., HXT1 or MIG1).
evidence: This describes a classification of the observed gene expression landscapes.

claim: The typical lengths of all gene expression landscapes for different reporter genes were remarkably close.
source: We defined and extracted the typical lengths of the peaking and switching landscapes (Figure 7b) and plotted them as function of the external glucose concentration (Figure 7c). The typical lengths of all of these landscapes for different reporter genes were remarkably close, despite the fact that we looked at different cellular components: a transcription factor (MIG1), glucose transporters (HXTs), metabolic enzymes (HXKs) and metabolic state reporters (SDH2, PDC1).
evidence: This describes an observation from the analysis, supported by figures.

claim: The colonies were structured into two regions: an actively growing region where cells divide abundantly and ferment glucose, and a quiescent area where cells do not divide much and have switched to respiratory metabolism.
source: Notably, we gained a global view of gene expression landscapes and their interrelationships along a monolayer colony. All data showed the colonies were structured into two regions with very different properties (Figure 7d): an actively growing region, where cells divide abundantly and ferment glucose, and a quiescent area, where cells do not divide much and have switched to respiratory metabolism to compensate for the very low glucose availability.
evidence: This describes a conclusion from the study, supported by a figure.

claim: Genetic programs enable multicellular assemblies to spatially self-organize through long-range metabolic interactions governed by physical rules of diffusion and uptake.
source: While it is not surprising to see the expression levels of metabolic genes vary with the glucose concentration, our approach demonstrates genetic programs not only allow individual cells to adapt to changes in the nutrient environment, but also enable multicellular assemblies to spatially self-organize through long-range metabolic interactions governed by physical rules of diffusion and uptake.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: All experiments were performed using haploid S. cerevisiae strains derived from the S288C background - BY4741.
source: All experiments were performed using haploid S. cerevisiae strains derived from the S288C background - BY4741: MATa his3Δ1 leu2Δ0 met15Δ0 ura3Δ0.
evidence: This describes the experimental materials used in the study.

claim: Microfluidic devices were constructed using soft lithography techniques.
source: Microfluidic devices were constructed using soft lithography techniques.
evidence: This describes the method used to fabricate the devices.

claim: Cells were precultured overnight in 5 mL of synthetic complete (SC) medium containing 2% w/vol glucose in a shaking incubator at 30°C.
source: Cells were precultured overnight in 5 mL of synthetic complete (SC) medium containing 2% w/vol glucose in a shaking incubator at 30°C, diluted 50-fold into 50 mL of SC +2% w/vol glucose, cultured for 5–6 hr in a shaking incubator at 30°C to an OD600 of 0.2–0.4, collected by centrifugation, and loaded into the microfluidic system with a pipette.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for cell preparation.

claim: The microfluidic system was centrifuged for 2 min at 1000 rpm to force the cells into the dead-end cell chambers.
source: The microfluidic system was centrifuged for 2 min at 1000 rpm using 3D-printed adaptors (Laurell WS-650 spin coater) to force the cells into the dead-end cell chambers.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for cell loading.

claim: Liquid media was flowed rapidly through the flow channel to remove excess cells and the flow rate was set to 5 µL/min.
source: Liquid media was flowed rapidly through the flow channel to remove excess cells and the flow rate was set to 5 µL/min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for media flow.

claim: Flow cytometry experiments were performed on a Gallios Flow Cytometer using a 488 nm excitation laser and 530/30 nm FL1 emission filter to detect GFP fluorescence.
source: Flow cytometry experiments were performed on a Gallios Flow Cytometer (Beckman Coulter) using a 488 nm excitation laser and 530/30 nm FL1 emission filter to detect GFP fluorescence.
evidence: This describes the experimental method for flow cytometry.

claim: Approximately 104 cells were inoculated in 10 mL of SC medium containing various glucose concentrations and cultured in a shaking incubator at 30°C to an OD600 of ~0.02–0.2.
source: Approximately 104 cells were inoculated in 10 mL of SC medium containing various glucose concentrations (log2 dilutions from 8% to 0.0078125%, and 0% w/vol glucose) and cultured in a shaking incubator at 30°C to an OD600 of ~0.02–0.2 depending on the starting glucose concentration.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for batch culture experiments.

claim: Cells were then diluted 10-fold into 10 mL of fresh SC media containing the same starting glucose concentration and grown for 4–5 hr in a shaking incubator at 30°C.
source: Cells were then diluted 10-fold into 10 mL of fresh SC media containing the same starting glucose concentration and grown for 4–5 hr in a shaking incubator at 30°C, centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 10 min, re-suspended in 300 µL of PBS pH 7.4 buffer (Gibco) and fluorescence was measured using the flow cytometer.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for batch culture experiments.

claim: The glucose concentration remained at similar levels during the growth phase in batch culture experiments.
source: The supernatant of each sample was collected, and the glucose concentration was measured using the Glucose (HK) Assay Kit (Sigma) to confirm that the glucose concentration remained at similar levels during the growth phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This describes a control measurement performed in the study, supported by a figure.

claim: Image analysis was performed using open-source ImageJ 1.51 p software.
source: Image analysis was performed using open-source ImageJ 1.51 p software (Schneider et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the software used for image analysis.

claim: TrackMate v3.5.1 was used to track cell trajectories to compute the local speed of the cells inside the cell assembly.
source: To compute the local speed of the cells inside the cell assembly, we used the plugin TrackMate (Tinevez et al., 2017) v3.5.1 to track cell trajectories.
evidence: This describes the software used for cell tracking analysis.
